question: When may an existing KYC-compliant customer open another account or use another service at the same RE without repeating customer identification?
reference_answer: Under the RBI KYC Direction the CDD procedure is applied at the UCIC level, so if an existing KYC-compliant customer of an RE wants to open another account or use another product or service from the same RE, no fresh CDD is needed as far as identification of the customer is concerned (para 10(f), Customer Acceptance Policy).
required_facts: F1::CDD is applied at the UCIC level;F2::The customer must be an existing KYC-compliant customer of the same RE;F3::The customer may open another account or avail another product or service from the same RE;F4::No fresh CDD exercise is needed as far as identification of the customer is concerned
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 10(f), p19 (amended Nov 6, 2024). Draft's 'no change in identity or address' and 'RE can retrieve KYC record' conditions are NOT in the text and were removed.

question: In which circumstances must a regulated entity identify a customer under the KYC Direction?
reference_answer: Under para 13 an RE must identify customers: (a) on commencement of an account-based relationship; (b) when carrying out international money transfer operations for a person who is not an account holder; (c) when there is doubt about the authenticity or adequacy of customer identification data already obtained; (d) when selling third party products as agent, selling own products, paying dues of credit cards or selling and reloading prepaid or travel cards, or any other product, for more than Rs 50,000; (e) for a walk-in non-account-based customer where the amount equals or exceeds Rs 50,000 whether in a single transaction or several connected ones; (f) when the RE believes a customer is intentionally structuring transactions below Rs 50,000. Para 13(g) adds that introduction is not to be sought when opening accounts.
required_facts: F1::Identification is required at commencement of an account-based relationship;F2::Identification is required for international money transfer operations for a non-account-holder;F3::Identification is required when there is doubt about authenticity or adequacy of customer identification data obtained;F4::Identification is required when selling third party or own products or card dues or prepaid card sales for more than Rs 50000;F5::Identification is required for a walk-in customer transaction of Rs 50000 or more whether single or connected transactions;F6::Identification is required where the RE believes the customer is structuring transactions below the Rs 50000 threshold
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 13(a)-(g), p22. Draft F4 was a placeholder; replaced with the actual triggers. 13(g) (no introduction) is not an identification trigger and is noted in the answer only.

question: What conditions must a regulated entity satisfy when relying on a third party to perform customer due diligence?
reference_answer: Para 14 lets an RE, at its option, rely on CDD done by a third party when verifying identity at commencement of an account-based relationship, for an occasional transaction of Rs 50,000 or more (single or connected), or for international money transfer operations, subject to: (a) CDD records or information are obtained immediately from the third party or from CKYCR; (b) adequate steps ensure copies of identification data and other CDD documentation will be made available from the third party on request without delay; (c) the third party is regulated, supervised or monitored for, and has measures for, CDD and record-keeping compliance in line with PML Act requirements; (d) the third party is not based in a country or jurisdiction assessed as high risk; (e) ultimate responsibility for CDD and enhanced due diligence stays with the RE.
required_facts: F1::CDD records or information are obtained immediately from the third party or from CKYCR;F2::The RE takes adequate steps to ensure identification data copies and CDD documentation are available from the third party on request without delay;F3::The third party is regulated supervised or monitored and has CDD and record-keeping measures in line with the PML Act;F4::The third party is not based in a country or jurisdiction assessed as high risk;F5::Ultimate responsibility for CDD and enhanced due diligence remains with the RE
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 14(a)-(e), pp22-23. Draft omitted the high-risk jurisdiction condition and the 'at their option' scope; corrected.

question: How should the beneficial owner of a legal person be identified?
reference_answer: Para 34 (p38) requires the beneficial owner(s) of a legal person who is not a natural person to be identified and all reasonable steps under Rule 9(3) of the PML Rules taken to verify identity, except that for entities listed on an Indian stock exchange, listed in notified jurisdictions, or subsidiaries of such listed entities, identifying shareholders or beneficial owners is not necessary; for trust, nominee or fiduciary accounts the intermediary and the persons on whose behalf they act must be identified. Who counts as beneficial owner is defined in para 3(a)(iv) (pp5-6): for a company, natural person(s) with controlling ownership interest (more than 10 percent of shares, capital or profits) or control through other means; for a partnership firm, more than 10 percent of capital or profits or control; for an unincorporated association or body of individuals, more than 15 percent; for a trust, the author, trustees, beneficiaries with 10 percent or more interest and anyone with ultimate effective control; if no natural person is identified under the company, partnership or association tests, the relevant natural person who is the senior managing official.
required_facts: F1::The beneficial owner of a non-natural legal person must be identified and reasonable steps taken to verify identity under Rule 9(3) of the PML Rules;F2::For a company the beneficial owner is a natural person with controlling ownership interest of more than 10 percent of shares capital or profits or control through other means;F3::For a partnership firm the threshold is more than 10 percent of capital or profits and for an unincorporated association or body of individuals more than 15 percent;F4::If no natural person is identified under the company partnership or association tests the senior managing official is the beneficial owner;F5::Identification and verification of shareholders or beneficial owners is not necessary for Indian listed entities or listed-jurisdiction entities or their subsidiaries;F6::For trust nominee or fiduciary accounts evidence of identity of the intermediaries and the persons on whose behalf they act and the nature of the trust arrangement must be obtained
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Gold passage (p38) only has para 34; the thresholds and senior-managing-official fallback are in the definition, para 3(a)(iv), pp5-6, so gold was supplemented. Draft F2/F3 had no figures and the fallback was uncited.

question: What are the requirements for enhanced due diligence?
reference_answer: Part VI A (pp45-46) sets out enhanced due diligence for non-face-to-face onboarding (para 40): V-CIP offered first if available; no alternate mobile numbers linked after CDD and transactions only from the account-opening mobile number, with a Board-approved policy for mobile-number changes; current address verified through positive confirmation before operations are allowed; PAN obtained and verified; first transaction a credit from the customer's existing KYC-complied bank account; customer categorised high risk and subject to enhanced monitoring until identity is verified face-to-face or via V-CIP. Para 41 adds EDD for PEPs (risk-management system to identify PEPs, reasonable measures on source of funds or wealth, senior management approval to open or continue, enhanced ongoing monitoring, extended to family members and close associates).
required_facts: F1::For non-face-to-face onboarding V-CIP if available is offered first to the customer;F2::Alternate mobile numbers are not linked post CDD and transactions are permitted only from the mobile number used for account opening with a Board-approved policy for change of mobile number;F3::Current address is verified through positive confirmation before allowing operations in the account;F4::PAN is obtained and verified from the issuing authority verification facility;F5::The first transaction in the account is a credit from the customer's existing KYC-complied bank account;F6::Such customers are categorised high-risk and subject to enhanced monitoring until identity is verified face-to-face or through V-CIP;F7::For PEPs the RE needs a risk management system source of funds or wealth measures senior management approval and enhanced ongoing monitoring
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Paras 40-41, pp45-46. Verified scope is the EDD provisions of Part VI A; other EDD references (e.g. correspondent banking p56, para 37 p39) are separate. Draft was generic with no specific measures.

question: What confidentiality obligations apply to customer information?
reference_answer: Para 55 (p57): REs must keep customer information arising from the contractual relationship secret; information collected for opening an account is confidential and may not be divulged for cross-selling or any other purpose without the customer's express permission; when Government or other agencies request information the RE must be satisfied it does not violate secrecy laws; exceptions are disclosure under compulsion of law, a duty to the public to disclose, where the RE's interest requires disclosure, and with the customer's express or implied consent.
required_facts: F1::REs must maintain secrecy of customer information arising from the contractual relationship;F2::Information collected for account opening is confidential and not divulged for cross-selling or any other purpose without the customer's express permission;F3::On requests from Government or agencies the RE must satisfy itself the request does not violate secrecy laws;F4::Exceptions are compulsion of law and a duty to the public to disclose and where the RE's interest requires disclosure and with express or implied customer consent
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 55(a)-(d), p57.

question: How quickly must KYC records be uploaded to CKYCR after starting an account-based relationship?
reference_answer: Under para 56(b) and Rule 9(1A) of the PML Rules, an RE must capture the customer's KYC records and upload them onto CKYCR within 10 days of commencement of an account-based relationship.
required_facts: F1::The RE must capture the customer's KYC records and upload them onto CKYCR;F2::The deadline is within 10 days of commencement of the account-based relationship
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 56(b), p58. Draft was correct in substance; made precise.

question: What must an RE do when CKYCR provides an updated KYC record?
reference_answer: Under para 56(h) (pp58-59), when the RE obtains additional or updated customer information it must furnish it to CKYCR within seven days (or any period notified by the Central Government), after which CKYCR informs all reporting entities that dealt with the customer. Once CKYCR informs an RE of an update to an existing customer's KYC record, the RE shall retrieve the updated record from CKYCR and update its own KYC record.
required_facts: F1::CKYCR informs reporting entities electronically of an update to a customer's KYC record;F2::The RE must retrieve the updated KYC records from CKYCR;F3::The RE must update the KYC record maintained by the RE;F4::An RE that obtains updated information from a customer must furnish it to CKYCR within seven days or such period as the Central Government notifies
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 56(h) spans pp58-59; gold had p59 only so gold was widened. Draft did not cover the 7-day onward-furnishing duty.

question: What information is required for cross-border wire transfers?
reference_answer: Para 64A (pp63-64): all cross-border wire transfers must carry accurate, complete and meaningful originator and beneficiary information: originator name; originator account number where an account is used; originator address or national identity number or customer identification number or date and place of birth; beneficiary name; beneficiary account number where an account is used. Without an account a unique transaction reference number permitting traceability must be included. Batch transfers are exempt from the per-transfer originator information if they carry the originator account number or unique reference number and the batch file has full originator and beneficiary information traceable in the beneficiary country. Domestic wire transfers by account holders carry the same information; domestic transfers of Rs 50,000 and above by non-account holders also need it, while below Rs 50,000 a unique transaction reference may suffice if information can be made available by other means within three working days of a request.
required_facts: F1::Cross-border wire transfers must carry originator name and account number where used and originator address or national identity number or customer identification number or date and place of birth;F2::Cross-border wire transfers must carry beneficiary name and beneficiary account number where used;F3::Without an account a unique transaction reference number permitting traceability must be included;F4::Batch transfers are exempt from per-transfer originator information if they carry the account number or unique reference and the batch file contains required originator and full beneficiary information;F5::Domestic wire transfers below Rs 50000 by a non-account holder may include only a unique transaction reference number and the ordering RE must make information available within three working days of a request
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). The information list is in para 64A on pp63-64; gold 64-67 missed p63 (where it starts). Gold widened. Pp65-67 cover responsibilities of ordering, intermediary and beneficiary REs and other obligations, not the information list.

question: What are the requirements for PAN or Form 60 when carrying out applicable transactions?
reference_answer: Para 66 (p68): PAN or its equivalent e-document must be obtained and verified for transactions covered by Income Tax Rule 114B applicable to banks, as amended from time to time; Form 60 must be obtained from persons who do not have PAN or its equivalent e-document.
required_facts: F1::PAN or equivalent e-document is obtained and verified while undertaking transactions as per Income Tax Rule 114B applicable to banks;F2::Form 60 is obtained from persons who do not have PAN or equivalent e-document
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 66, p68. Draft F3 (verify 'as prescribed') merged into F1 since text says 'obtained and verified'. Applicable transactions are those under Rule 114B (not enumerated in this Direction); see also para 67(d) p68 for third-party product sales.

question: What controls apply to the digital KYC application used at customer touch points?
reference_answer: Annex I (p71) requires: an RE-developed digital KYC application available at customer touch points, with KYC done only through it; access controlled by the RE via login-id and password or Live OTP or Time OTP for authorised officials and not usable by unauthorised persons; live photograph of the customer taken by the authorised officer and embedded in the CAF, watermarked with CAF number, GPS coordinates, officer name, unique employee code, date and time; only a live photograph captured (no printed or video-graphed photograph), white background and no other person in frame; live photograph of the original OVD (or proof of possession of Aadhaar) captured vertically from above with watermark and no skew or tilt; proper light for readability; CAF entries filled as per documents with QR-code auto-population permitted.
required_facts: F1::The RE must develop a digital KYC application available at customer touch points and KYC is undertaken only through it;F2::Access is controlled by the RE and limited to authorised officials via login-id and password or Live OTP or Time OTP;F3::A live photograph of the customer is taken by the authorised officer embedded in the CAF and watermarked with CAF number GPS coordinates officer name employee code date and time;F4::Only a live photograph is captured with no printed or video-graphed photograph and a white background with no other person in frame;F5::The original OVD or proof of possession of Aadhaar is photographed live placed horizontally and captured vertically from above with watermark and no skew or tilt
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Annex I paras A-H, p71 (continues on p72). Draft was generic ('controls'); replaced with the actual controls.

question: What is the role of OTP in the digital KYC process?
reference_answer: Annex I paras I-J (p72): after the CAF is completed an OTP message ('Please verify the details filled in form before sharing OTP') is sent to the customer's own mobile number and on successful validation is treated as the customer's signature on the CAF; if the customer has no mobile number, that of a family member, relative or known person may be used and must be mentioned in the CAF, but never the authorised officer's registered mobile number. The authorised officer separately declares capture of the live photograph and document, verified by an OTP to the officer's RE-registered mobile, which is treated as the officer's signature on the declaration.
required_facts: F1::An OTP is sent to the customer's own mobile number after the CAF is completed and on successful validation is treated as the customer's signature on the CAF;F2::If the customer lacks a mobile number the number of family relatives or known persons may be used and must be mentioned in the CAF;F3::The authorised officer's registered mobile number must not be used for the customer's signature;F4::The authorised officer's declaration is verified by an OTP sent to the officer's RE-registered mobile number and that OTP validation is treated as the officer's signature
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Annex I paras I-J, p72.

question: What training requirements apply to staff involved in KYC and AML/CFT activities?
reference_answer: Para 70 (pp69-70): REs must have a Know Your Employee screening mechanism in hiring; endeavour to ensure staff handling KYC/AML/CFT have integrity, understanding of standards and communication skills; and put in place an on-going employee training programme so staff are adequately trained in KYC/AML/CFT policy, with training focus differing for frontline staff, compliance staff and staff dealing with new customers; front-desk staff are to be specially trained to handle issues arising from lack of customer education; audit function must be staffed with adequately trained persons.
required_facts: F1::An on-going employee training programme must be in place so staff are adequately trained in KYC/AML/CFT policy;F2::Training focus differs for frontline staff and compliance staff and staff dealing with new customers;F3::Front desk staff are specially trained to handle issues arising from lack of customer education;F4::The audit function must be staffed with persons adequately trained and well-versed in KYC/AML/CFT policies
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 70(c) pp69-70; para 70(a)-(b) cover hiring screening and staff qualities (noted in answer).

question: What additional controls apply when establishing or continuing a relationship with a politically exposed person (PEP)?
reference_answer: Para 41 (p46): an RE may establish a relationship with a PEP (customer or beneficial owner) if, besides normal CDD: it has an appropriate risk management system to determine whether the customer or beneficial owner is a PEP; takes reasonable measures to establish source of funds or wealth; obtains senior management approval to open the account; subjects the account to enhanced on-going monitoring; and, if an existing customer or beneficial owner later becomes a PEP, obtains senior management approval to continue the relationship. The instructions also apply to family members or close associates of PEPs. PEPs are individuals who are or have been entrusted with prominent public functions by a foreign country.
required_facts: F1::The RE must have an appropriate risk management system to determine whether the customer or beneficial owner is a PEP;F2::The RE must take reasonable measures to establish source of funds or wealth;F3::Senior management approval is required to open an account for a PEP;F4::All PEP accounts are subject to enhanced on-going monitoring;F5::If an existing customer or beneficial owner subsequently becomes a PEP senior management approval is required to continue the relationship;F6::The requirements also apply to family members or close associates of PEPs
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 41A-B and Explanation, p46.

question: When may an RE require a customer to resubmit KYC records already available through CKYCR?
reference_answer: Para 56(j) (p59): for establishing an account-based relationship, updation or periodic updation, or identity verification, the RE shall seek or retrieve the customer's KYC Identifier from CKYCR and obtain KYC records online, and shall not require the customer to submit the same records or additional identification documents unless: (i) the customer's information has changed from CKYCR's records; (ii) the retrieved record is incomplete or not per current KYC norms; (iii) the validity period of downloaded documents has lapsed; or (iv) the RE considers it necessary to verify identity or address (including current address), to perform enhanced due diligence or to build an appropriate risk profile.
required_facts: F1::The RE must seek or retrieve the KYC Identifier from CKYCR and obtain KYC records online and not ask the customer to resubmit the same records;F2::Resubmission may be required where there is a change in customer information compared with CKYCR records;F3::Resubmission may be required where the retrieved record is incomplete or not as per current KYC norms;F4::Resubmission may be required where the validity period of downloaded documents has lapsed;F5::Resubmission may be required where the RE considers it necessary to verify identity or address or perform EDD or build a risk profile
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 56(j), p59 holds the four exceptions; p58 is the preceding CKYCR context only.

question: For Category I FPIs, are constitutive documents mandatory according to the KYC table?
reference_answer: Yes. In the Annex IV table (p94), Constitutive Documents (Memorandum and Articles of Association, Certificate of Incorporation etc.) at entity level are marked Mandatory for Category I (as for Categories II and III).
required_facts: F1::Constitutive documents are Mandatory for Category I FPIs at entity level
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Annex IV p94, row 'Constitutive Documents', column Category I = Mandatory. Table inspected as image and text.

question: According to the FPI KYC table, is proof of address mandatory for Category III entities?
reference_answer: Yes, but with a carve-out. At entity level proof of address is marked 'Mandatory other than Power of Attorney' for Category III, meaning a PoA mentioning the address is not accepted as address proof for Category III, unlike Categories I and II where such a PoA is acceptable (Annex IV, p94).
required_facts: F1::Proof of address is Mandatory for Category III entities;F2::For Category III a Power of Attorney is not acceptable as address proof whereas for Categories I and II a PoA mentioning the address is acceptable
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Annex IV p94, entity-level 'Proof of Address' row, Category III cell reads 'Mandatory other than Power of Attorney'.

question: What does the KYC table specify about photographs for eligible FPIs?
reference_answer: Photographs are Exempted for Category I and Category II FPIs and marked 'Exempted *' for Category III for senior management, authorised signatories and UBO (the table has no entity-level photograph row); the asterisk means not required while opening the bank account, though the FPI may give an undertaking to submit the document on demand by regulators or law enforcement (Annex IV, pp94-95).
required_facts: F1::Photographs are Exempted for Category I and Category II FPIs;F2::Photographs are marked Exempted with an asterisk for Category III;F3::The asterisk means not required while opening the account but an undertaking to submit on demand by regulators or law enforcement agencies may be given
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Photograph rows for senior management, authorised signatories and UBO appear on p95; the asterisk note is at the foot of p95. Table inspected as image.

question: For Category III FPIs, is proof of identity mandatory for the ultimate beneficial owner (UBO)?
reference_answer: Yes. For Category III FPIs, proof of identity of the Ultimate Beneficial Owner is marked Mandatory (for Categories I and II it is Exempted *, i.e. not required while opening the account) (Annex IV, p95).
required_facts: F1::Proof of identity for the UBO is Mandatory for Category III FPIs
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). UBO / Proof of Identity row is on p95 only (the UBO block starts p95). Table inspected as image. Gold narrowed from 94;95 to 95.

question: For Category III FPIs, what does the table require for the list of authorized signatories and their signatures?
reference_answer: For Category III FPIs, the List and Signatures of authorised signatories is marked Mandatory (Annex IV, p95). For Categories I and II it is Mandatory too, with a note that a list of Global Custodian signatories can be given where there is a PoA to a Global Custodian.
required_facts: F1::The list and signatures of authorised signatories are Mandatory for Category III FPIs
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Authorised Signatories / List and Signatures row is on p95 only. Table inspected as image. Gold narrowed from 94;95 to 95.

question: Who remains responsible for compliance when an RE uses a Lending Service Provider or Digital Lending App?
reference_answer: The RE remains responsible. Para 2 of the circular says outsourcing to an LSP or DLA does not diminish the RE's obligations, the RE must continue to conform to the extant outsourcing guidelines, and must ensure LSPs and DLAs (of the RE or of the LSP) comply with the circular's guidelines. Note: the circular carries a banner on p1 stating it has been repealed and replaced by the RBI (Digital Lending) Directions, 2025 dated May 8, 2025.
required_facts: F1::Outsourcing to an LSP or DLA does not diminish the RE's obligations;F2::The RE must continue to conform to extant outsourcing guidelines;F3::The RE must ensure LSPs and DLAs comply with the guidelines in the circular
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 2, p1. Repeal banner on p1 is a currency qualification.

question: By what date were REs required to put systems in place for existing digital loans to comply with the 2022 guidelines?
reference_answer: By November 30, 2022. The circular (dated September 2, 2022) applies to existing customers availing fresh loans and new customers from its date, and REs were given until November 30, 2022 to put adequate systems and processes in place so that existing digital loans sanctioned as on the date of the circular also comply.
required_facts: F1::The deadline for existing digital loans was November 30 2022;F2::It covered existing digital loans sanctioned as on the date of the circular;F3::The instructions applied from the circular date to existing customers availing fresh loans and to new customers
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 3, pp1-2 (para 3 starts on p1 and the deadline sentence is on p2).

question: Who should pay fees or charges payable to a Lending Service Provider in the digital lending process?
reference_answer: The RE. Para 4.1 requires REs to pay fees and charges payable to LSPs directly, and such fees are not to be charged by the LSP to the borrower directly.
required_facts: F1::Fees and charges payable to LSPs are paid directly by the RE;F2::They are not charged by the LSP to the borrower directly
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 4.1, p4.

question: What information must be disclosed through the Key Fact Statement for a digital loan?
reference_answer: Para 5.2 (p5): the RE must give a standardised Key Fact Statement before contract execution (format in Annex II). Apart from other necessary information it must contain the APR, the recovery mechanism, details of the grievance redressal officer designated for digital lending or FinTech matters, and the cooling-off or look-up period. APR as all-inclusive cost must also be disclosed upfront (para 5.1) and penal charge rates must be disclosed upfront on an annualised basis in the KFS (para 4.2, p4). Fees not mentioned in the KFS cannot be charged at any stage (5.2.3).
required_facts: F1::The KFS must be given before execution of the contract in a standardised format;F2::The KFS contains the APR;F3::The KFS contains the recovery mechanism;F4::The KFS contains details of the grievance redressal officer for digital lending or FinTech matters;F5::The KFS contains the cooling-off or look-up period;F6::Fees or charges not mentioned in the KFS cannot be charged to the borrower during the loan
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 5.2, p5; penal charge disclosure in KFS is para 4.2 on p4.

question: For commercial banks, what is the deadline for submitting all audited returns under the revised filing requirements?
reference_answer: For commercial banks, the revised guideline for All Audited Returns is within 5 working days from the date of signing of the Auditor's report under section 134 of the Companies Act, 2013 (earlier: within 7 days from completion of the statutory audit of books of accounts).
required_facts: F1::The revised deadline for all audited returns of commercial banks is within 5 working days;F2::The period runs from the date of signing of the Auditor's report under section 134 of the Companies Act 2013
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Annex summary table, p1 (page footer shows '5'), row 'All Audited Returns' under 'Changes in instructions for Commercial Banks'. Document is bilingual Hindi/English; English table inspected as text.

question: How often must periodic KYC updation be carried out for high-risk, medium-risk and low-risk customers?
reference_answer: Para 38 (p39): REs adopt a risk-based approach to periodic KYC updation, but updation must be carried out at least once every two years for high-risk customers, every eight years for medium-risk customers and every ten years for low-risk customers, counted from the date of account opening or last KYC updation; the policy must be documented in the RE's internal KYC policy.
required_facts: F1::High-risk customers are updated at least once every two years;F2::Medium-risk customers are updated at least once every eight years;F3::Low-risk customers are updated at least once every ten years;F4::The period runs from the date of opening of the account or last KYC updation
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 38, p39.

question: What limits apply to credits, withdrawals and balance in a small account?
reference_answer: Para 23 (p32) small account: aggregate credits in a financial year not above Rs 1 lakh; aggregate withdrawals and transfers in a month not above Rs 10,000; balance at any time not above Rs 50,000 (the balance limit is not considered for deposits of Government grants, welfare benefits and payments against procurements).
required_facts: F1::Aggregate credits in a financial year do not exceed Rs 1 lakh;F2::Aggregate withdrawals and transfers in a month do not exceed Rs 10000;F3::Balance at any point of time does not exceed Rs 50000;F4::The balance limit is not applied to deposits of Government grants or welfare benefits or payments against procurements
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 23, p32.

question: How soon after becoming aware of a personal data breach must a data fiduciary give the Board detailed information about it?
reference_answer: Under Rule 7(2) of the DPDP Rules, on becoming aware of a breach the data fiduciary must intimate the Board without delay with a description of the breach, and within seventy-two hours of becoming aware (or within a longer period the Board allows on written request) give updated and detailed information, including broad facts and reasons, mitigation measures, findings about the person who caused it, remedial measures and a report on intimations to affected Data Principals.
required_facts: F1::The detailed information must be given within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach;F2::The Board may allow a longer period on a written request;F3::The detailed information includes the broad facts and reasons and mitigation measures and findings about who caused the breach and remedial measures and a report on intimations to Data Principals;F4::A description of the breach must be intimated to the Board without delay
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Rule 7(2)(a)-(b), p26.

question: What minimum net worth must an applicant have to register as a Consent Manager?
reference_answer: A Consent Manager applicant must have a net worth of not less than two crore rupees (First Schedule, Part A, item 4, referred to by Rule 4), in addition to being a company incorporated in India and meeting the other listed conditions.
required_facts: F1::Net worth must be not less than Rs 2 crore;F2::The condition is in Part A of the First Schedule as a condition for registration of a Consent Manager

question: When does Rule 4 of the DPDP Rules come into force, and how does that differ from the commencement of rules 3 and 5 to 16?
reference_answer: Rule 1(3): Rule 4 comes into force one year after the date of publication of the Gazette notification (published November 13, 2025). Rule 1(4): rules 3, 5 to 16, 22 and 23 come into force eighteen months after publication. Rule 1(2): rules 1, 2 and 17 to 21 came into force on publication.
required_facts: F1::Rule 4 comes into force one year after the date of publication of the Gazette;F2::Rules 3 and 5 to 16 and 22 and 23 come into force eighteen months after publication;F3::Rules 1 and 2 and 17 to 21 come into force on publication
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Rule 1(2)-(4), p24 (notification dated Nov 13, 2025). Exact calendar dates are computed, not stated, in the source.

question: What is the window a borrower gets to exit a digital loan they decide not to continue with, and who decides how long it is?
reference_answer: Para 8 of Annex I (p7): a borrower must be given an explicit option to exit a digital loan by paying the principal and the proportionate APR without any penalty during the cooling-off or look-up period. The period is determined by the RE's Board but must be not less than three days for loans of tenor seven days or more and one day for loans of tenor less than seven days. The definition (para 2.2, p3) also says the Board determines the window.
required_facts: F1::The borrower has an explicit option to exit the digital loan during the cooling-off or look-up period;F2::Exit is by paying the principal and the proportionate APR without any penalty;F3::The RE's Board determines the period;F4::The period must be not less than three days for loans of tenor seven days or more and one day for loans of tenor less than seven days
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Gold passage p3 has only the definition. The exit mechanism and minimum durations are in para 8 on p7, so gold was supplemented. Draft facts were substantively right.

question: On what amount may penal interest be charged on a digital loan?
reference_answer: Para 4.2 (p4): penal interest or charges on borrowers must be based on the outstanding amount of the loan, and the rate must be disclosed upfront on an annualised basis in the Key Fact Statement.
required_facts: F1::Penal interest or charges are based on the outstanding amount of the loan;F2::The rate of penal charges is disclosed upfront on an annualised basis in the KFS
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 4.2, p4.

question: Which documents must automatically reach the borrower by email or SMS once a digital loan contract is executed?
reference_answer: Para 5.3 (p5): digitally signed documents on the RE's letter head, namely the KFS, summary of loan product, sanction letter, terms and conditions, account statements and the privacy policies of the LSPs or DLAs with respect to borrower data, must automatically flow to the borrower's registered and verified email or SMS upon execution of the loan contract.
required_facts: F1::Documents are digitally signed on the RE's letter head;F2::The documents are the KFS and summary of loan product and sanction letter and terms and conditions and account statements and privacy policies of the LSPs or DLAs;F3::They flow automatically to the borrower's registered and verified email or SMS upon execution of the loan contract
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 5.3, p5.

question: Under the PFRDA KYC/AML/CFT master circular, how is the Video Based Customer Identification Process defined?
reference_answer: PFRDA master circular para 3.26 (p6, as amended): VCIP is an alternate method of customer identification with facial recognition and client due diligence by an authorised official of the RE, through seamless, secure, live, informed-consent based audio-visual interaction with the subscriber, to obtain identification information required for CDD and to ascertain the veracity of the information furnished through independent verification, while maintaining an audit trail.
required_facts: F1::VCIP is an alternate method of customer identification with facial recognition and client due diligence;F2::It is carried out by an authorised official of the RE;F3::It involves seamless secure live informed-consent based audio-visual interaction with the subscriber;F4::Its purpose is to obtain identification information for CDD and verify the information through independent verification;F5::An audit trail of the process is maintained
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 3.26, p6. Draft said 'in accordance with the PFRDA circular's prescribed procedure', which is not in the definition; replaced.

question: Under the RBI KYC Direction, how is the Video based Customer Identification Process (V-CIP) defined?
reference_answer: RBI KYC Direction para 3(b)(xvi) (p13): V-CIP is an alternate method of customer identification with facial recognition and CDD by an authorised official of the RE, through seamless, secure, live, informed-consent based audio-visual interaction with the customer, to obtain identification information for CDD and ascertain its veracity through independent verification, maintaining an audit trail; processes complying with prescribed standards and procedures are treated on par with face-to-face CIP.
required_facts: F1::V-CIP is an alternate method of customer identification with facial recognition and CDD;F2::It is carried out by an authorised official of the RE through live informed-consent based audio-visual interaction with the customer;F3::It is used to obtain identification information for CDD and to ascertain its veracity through independent verification;F4::An audit trail of the process is maintained;F5::Compliant V-CIP is treated on par with face-to-face CIP for the Master Direction
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Definition xvi, p13. Draft's 'record-retention controls' not in the definition; replaced with audit trail and on-par-with-face-to-face.

question: For how long can accounts opened through Aadhaar OTP based e-KYC operate before further identification is required?
reference_answer: Para 17(vi)-(vii) (p27): accounts, deposit and borrowal, opened through Aadhaar OTP based e-KYC in non-face-to-face mode are not allowed for more than one year unless identification under para 16 or V-CIP under para 18 is carried out (using Aadhaar under para 18 requires the full process including fresh Aadhaar OTP authentication). If not completed within a year, deposit accounts are closed immediately and borrowal accounts get no further debits.
required_facts: F1::Such accounts are not allowed for more than one year unless further identification is completed;F2::Further identification is under paragraph 16 or V-CIP under paragraph 18;F3::If CDD is not completed within a year deposit accounts are closed immediately and borrowal accounts get no further debits
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 17(vi)-(vii), p27.

question: How do the balance and annual credit limits for Aadhaar OTP based e-KYC accounts differ from the limits on small accounts?
reference_answer: Aadhaar OTP e-KYC accounts (para 17, pp26-27): aggregate balance of all deposit accounts not above Rs 1 lakh (account ceases to be operational if exceeded until CDD is done); aggregate credits in a financial year across all deposit accounts not above Rs 2 lakh; term loans only, aggregate not above Rs 60,000 a year; valid for one year unless further CDD is done. Small accounts (para 23, p32): balance not above Rs 50,000 at any time; credits in a financial year not above Rs 1 lakh; withdrawals and transfers not above Rs 10,000 a month. So the OTP e-KYC limits are higher on balance (Rs 1 lakh vs Rs 50,000) and annual credits (Rs 2 lakh vs Rs 1 lakh), and add a Rs 60,000 term-loan cap; the small account additionally caps monthly withdrawals at Rs 10,000, which the OTP e-KYC provision does not.
required_facts: F1::Aadhaar OTP e-KYC accounts have an aggregate deposit balance limit of Rs 1 lakh whereas small accounts have a balance limit of Rs 50000;F2::Aadhaar OTP e-KYC accounts have an annual aggregate credit limit of Rs 2 lakh whereas small accounts have Rs 1 lakh;F3::Aadhaar OTP e-KYC borrowal accounts allow only term loans up to Rs 60000 a year;F4::Small accounts cap withdrawals and transfers at Rs 10000 a month and the OTP e-KYC provision states no equivalent cap
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Para 17(iii)-(v), pp26-27; para 23, p32. F4 is a fact about absence in para 17: para 17 was read in full on pp26-27 and no monthly withdrawal cap is stated.

question: For how long must a data fiduciary keep logs and personal data so that unauthorised access can be detected and investigated?
reference_answer: Rule 6(1)(e) (p26): to enable detection of unauthorised access, its investigation, remediation to prevent recurrence and continued processing, the data fiduciary must retain the relevant logs and personal data for one year, unless compliance with any law requires otherwise. Rule 8(3) (p27) separately requires retaining personal data, associated traffic data and other logs for a minimum of one year from the date of processing.
required_facts: F1::The retention period is one year;F2::The retained material includes logs and personal data;F3::The purpose is detection and investigation of unauthorised access and remediation and continued processing;F4::Retention may be longer where another law requires
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Rule 6(1)(e), p26 (primary); Rule 8(3), p27 (related one-year minimum).

question: How far ahead of erasing personal data must the data principal be warned if they have not used the service?
reference_answer: Rule 8(2) (p27): at least forty-eight hours before the end of the time period for erasure under rule 8, the data fiduciary must inform the data principal that the personal data will be erased on completion of that period unless she logs into her user account or otherwise initiates contact for the specified purpose or exercises her rights. Rule 8 applies to classes of data fiduciaries and purposes specified in the Third Schedule, where the data principal neither approaches the fiduciary nor exercises her rights within the corresponding Third Schedule period.
required_facts: F1::The notice must be given at least 48 hours before completion of the period for erasure;F2::The trigger is that the data principal neither approaches the data fiduciary for the specified purpose nor exercises her rights within the Third Schedule period for that class and purpose;F3::The notice tells the data principal that the data will be erased unless she logs into her user account or initiates contact or exercises her rights
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Rule 8(1)-(2), p27. Draft's 'prescribed period of non-use' replaced with the Third Schedule trigger; Third Schedule periods themselves were not read for this question.

question: Where can an investor take a complaint about a research analyst if the analyst's own response does not satisfy them?
reference_answer: Under the 2026 SEBI Research Analysts Master Circular, an investor may lodge a grievance against a research analyst through SEBI's SCORES 2.0 platform at https://scores.sebi.gov.in. Complaints against research analysts follow a two-level review (first by the Research Analyst Administration and Supervisory Body, then by SEBI). For physical complaints, the circular provides the address of SEBI's Office of Investor Assistance and Education at SEBI Bhavan, Bandra-Kurla Complex, Mumbai.
required_facts: F1::The investor may lodge the grievance through SEBI's SCORES platform;F2::The current platform address is scores.sebi.gov.in;F3::The grievance route applies when the investor is dissatisfied with the research analyst's response;F4::The circular provides an alternative physical-complaint route to SEBI's Office of Investor Assistance and Education in Mumbai.
review_notes: Updated the gold source to the 2026 SEBI Research Analysts Master Circular after comparing the retrieved current passage with the older circular. The current source specifies SCORES 2.0, a two-level RAASB/SEBI review, and the physical-complaint address. The superseded scores.gov.in URL and older helpline are not carried forward as current facts.

question: Can a person who subscribed to the Special Bearer Bonds be made to disclose how they obtained them?
reference_answer: No, with exceptions. Section 3(1)(a) of the Special Bearer Bonds (Immunities and Exemptions) Ordinance, 1981 (p2) says that, notwithstanding any other law, no person who has subscribed to or otherwise acquired the Bonds is required to disclose, for any purpose whatsoever, the nature and source of acquisition. Section 3(1)(b)-(c) bar inquiry or investigation on that ground and make the fact inadmissible as evidence. Section 3(2): this does not apply to prosecution for offences under Chapter IX or XVII of the IPC, the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, or similar offences, or to enforcement of civil liability (which excludes liability by way of tax).
required_facts: F1::No person who subscribed to or otherwise acquired Special Bearer Bonds is required to disclose for any purpose the nature and source of acquisition;F2::The immunity applies notwithstanding anything in any other law;F3::The immunity does not apply to prosecution for offences under Chapter IX or XVII of the IPC or the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 or similar offences or to enforcement of civil liability;F4::Civil liability for this purpose does not include liability by way of tax
review_notes: Source-verified 2026-11-15 by Claude against PDF page text (pdftotext). Section 3, p2 (scanned page; read from page image and OCR). The instrument is an Ordinance (No. 1 of 1981), not an Act; the page carries a handwritten 'Repealed by ...' note at the top, so currency should be treated as superseded. Draft wording 'manner or consideration' was not in the text.
